summary: Specifies community requirements for choosing venues for IETF plenary meetings, including hotels and meeting space, and tells the IASA to make additional process documents available describing how meeting selection currently works.

plainLanguage.summary: This document tells the people who book the IETF's big meetings what a good venue has to offer. It lists a few rules that a place must meet, many things that are strongly preferred, and asks for the selection process to be published.

what is an ietf overflow hotel
subtitle: The community's requirements for choosing where the IETF holds its plenary meetings, from room size to travel visas.

tldr.problem: The IETF Administrative Support Activity arranges the plenary meeting venue on behalf of the community, and the community needed a shared, written set of standards for that choice.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8718 lists core values, a set of mandatory criteria that make a location unacceptable if unmet, a long list of important criteria, and lesser considerations, plus requirements for documenting the process.
tldr.outcome: Venue decisions become explainable and open to the community, with the IASA required to say when an important criterion could not be met. The RFC is a Best Current Practice from February 2020 and is updated by RFC 9712.

sections.title: Who Books the Meeting
sections.content:
The IETF Administrative Support Activity (IASA) is responsible for arranging the selection and operation of the IETF plenary meeting venue. This document guides the IASA in selecting regions, cities, facilities and hotels, and the IASA should apply the guidance at different points in the process to meet the requirements of the IETF community.

It remains the responsibility of the IASA to apply its best judgment. The IASA accepts input and feedback during the consultation process and later, for instance when the situation at a chosen location changes. The community is encouraged to give feedback about the IASA's performance to the IETF Administration LLC, the Nominations Committee (NOMCOM) or the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG).

Four terms describe the places for which the IETF contracts services. The Venue is an umbrella term for the city, meeting resources and guest room resources. The Facility is the building that houses meeting rooms and associated resources, and it may also house an IETF Hotel. The IETF Hotels are one or more hotels near the Facility where the guest room block is negotiated and where network services managed by the IASA, such as the "IETF" SSID, are in use. The Overflow Hotels are usually nearby hotels where the IETF has negotiated a group room rate; they are not usually connected to the IETF network and do not use IASA-managed network services.
sections.plainLanguage: A team inside the IETF does the booking. This document tells that team what to look for, so the community can see the reasons behind a choice. It also names the four kinds of place involved: the city, the building, the hotels with the IETF network, and the extra hotels further away.

sections.title: The Values Behind the Choice
sections.content:
Several values run through the whole selection process. Why we meet is the pursuit of the IETF's mission, partly by advancing the development of Internet-Drafts and RFCs, and also by enabling attendee participation in multiple topics and the cross-pollination of ideas and technologies.

Inclusiveness means facilitating the on-site or remote participation of anyone who wants to be involved, because widespread participation contributes to the diversity of perspectives in working sessions. Every country has limits on who it will admit, so the IETF seeks to minimize situations where onerous entry regulations inhibit, discourage or prevent participants from attending, and failing that to distribute meeting locations so that the same attendees do not always experience those regulations. It also seeks to avoid meeting in countries with laws that effectively exclude people on the basis of race, ethnicity, religion, gender, sexual orientation, national origin, citizenship or gender identity.

Where we meet means meeting in different global locations to spread the difficulty and cost of travel among active participants, balancing travel time and expense across regions, as set out in the regional location policy in RFC 8719.

Internet access is treated as a core value because the IETF writes specifications for the Internet and uses it heavily. Attendees need unfiltered access to the general Internet and their corporate networks, including access to corporate networks over encrypted VPNs from the meeting Facility and Hotels, and open network access at high enough data rates to support the work, which includes remote participation. The IETF is also the first user of its own technology, and filtering may cause problems with that technology development.

Focus means the meeting exists for focused technical discussions. These are not limited to scheduled breakout sessions; they also happen over meals or drinks, through a kind of non-session called a "Bar BOF", or in side meetings. Noisy or distracting environments reduce their effectiveness. Economics matters because many attendees are self-funded, so the IETF seeks locations with convenient budget alternatives for food and lodging and few travel segments from major airports. Least astonishment and openness means participants should not be surprised by venue selections, and the process should be as open as practicable so the community can discuss prospective selections well before a contract is considered.
sections.plainLanguage: Six or seven ideas shape every decision: the meeting exists to advance drafts, so many different people should be able to take part; the meetings should spread around the world so travel costs are shared; the Internet must work properly; the rooms must be quiet enough for real discussion; the trip must be affordable; and the process must be visible to the community.

sections.title: What the Choice Is Not For
sections.content: IETF meeting Venues are not selected or declined for three explicit purposes. Politics means endorsing or condemning particular countries, political paradigms, laws, regulations or policies. Maximal attendance is not a goal in itself: while the IETF strives to be as inclusive as possible, both online and in person, maximum attendance would defeat a key goal of the meeting if active contributors with differing points of view did not have the opportunity to resolve their disagreements, no matter how full the rooms. Tourism means variety in sightseeing experiences.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things are deliberately not the point: making a political statement, packing the rooms, and offering sightseeing. Disagreements between contributors need room to be worked out, which a huge crowd would prevent.

sections.title: The Mandatory Criteria
sections.content:
If the criteria in this section cannot be met, a location is unacceptable for selection and the IASA MUST NOT enter into a contract. If the IASA learns that a location can no longer meet a mandatory requirement after signing a contract, it will inform the community and address the matter case by case.

There are three such criteria. The Facility MUST provide sufficient space in an appropriate layout to accommodate the number of participants, leadership and support staff expected to attend. The Facility and IETF Hotels MUST provide wheelchair access to accommodate the number of people anticipated to require it. It MUST be possible to provision Internet access to the Facility and IETF Hotels that allows those attending in person to use the Internet for all their IETF, business and day-to-day needs, with sufficient bandwidth and access for remote attendees. That access includes native and unmodified IPv4 and IPv6 connectivity and global reachability, with no additional limitation that would materially affect their Internet use, and redundant paths to the Internet must be possible to ensure availability.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things are absolute. There must be enough room, there must be wheelchair access, and the Internet must work properly, with both IPv4 and IPv6, without filtering, and with a backup path in case one link fails.

sections.title: The Important Criteria
sections.content:
The criteria in this section are not mandatory, but they are highly significant. It may be necessary to trade one against another, and a Venue that meets more of them is preferable. Requirements classed as Important can also be balanced across Venue selections for multiple meetings. When a particular requirement here cannot be met but the Venue is selected anyway, the IASA MUST notify the community at the time of the venue announcement, and it may be appropriate to assist those who have been inconvenienced.

For the city: travel must be acceptable in cost, time and burden for participants from multiple regions, with the burden generally shared over several years; the Venue must be favorable for obtaining a host and sponsors; travel barriers to entry, including visa requirements, must be such that an overwhelming majority of participants who wish to attend can; economic, safety and health risks must be acceptable; and the selection must comport with the practices in RFC 8719.

For the Venue and Facilities: selected facilities SHALL have provided written assurance that they comply with local health, safety and accessibility laws and will remain in compliance for the whole stay. There must be enough places for ad hoc conversations within a walking distance of 5 to 10 minutes, and the cost of guest rooms, meeting space, food and drink must be affordable within the norms of business travel. The Facility must be accessible by people with disabilities, or reasonable accommodations must be possible.

For technical needs: the Facility's support technologies and services, such as network and audio-video, must be sufficient for the meeting, or the Facility must be willing to add them, or a third party may provide them, all at no or an acceptable cost. The IETF Hotels must directly provide, or permit and facilitate, a high performance, robust, unfiltered and unmodified Internet service for public areas and guest rooms, included in the cost of the room.

For hotels: they must be close to each other and to the Facility, and the guest rooms must be sufficient in number to house one-third or more of projected meeting attendees. Overflow Hotels must be placeable under contract within convenient travel time and at a variety of guest room rates, and budget hotels must exist nearby. At least one IETF Hotel or the Facility must have a lounge space conducive to planned and ad hoc meetings, with tables and seating convenient for small meetings with laptops.

For food and drink: the surroundings must offer convenient and inexpensive meals for a wide range of dietary requirements, reachable on foot, by short taxi ride or by local public transport; health-related and religion-related dietary requirements must be satisfiable through robust on-site service or an adequate grocery store; and grocery shopping must cover a wide range of dietary requirements nearby.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the points a good venue scores well on: an easy journey, few visa problems, a safe and affordable city, quiet nearby places to talk, internet in the hotels included in the room price, enough hotel rooms for a third of the attendees, and food that suits different diets. If one cannot be met, the IASA has to say so when it announces the venue.

sections.title: Publishing the Process
sections.content: The IETF Community works best when it is well informed. This memo does not specify processes nor who has responsibility for fulfilling the community's requirements for meetings, but both aspects are important. The IASA SHALL publicly document and keep current both a list of roles and responsibilities relating to IETF meetings and the selection processes used to fulfil the requirements of the community.
sections.plainLanguage: The IASA has to publish who does what and how the choice is made, and keep that document up to date.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This note proposes no protocols and therefore introduces no new protocol insecurities. It defines no protocol for anyone to attack.
sections.plainLanguage: There is no protocol here, so there is nothing new that can be attacked.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content: Different places have different constraints on individual privacy. The requirements in this memo are intended to provide for some limited protections. As meetings are announced, the IASA SHALL inform the IETF of any limitations to privacy they have become aware of in their investigations. Participants would be informed, for example, of any regulatory authentication or logging requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Laws differ from country to country about what can be recorded or logged. The IASA has to tell the community about any such limits it finds while checking out a city.
